passage:
Historians of labor have long debated the causes of the dramatic decline in working hours that occurred across industrialized nations during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The standard account, associated most prominently with the economic historian John Rae, holds that the reduction of the workday—from roughly twelve hours to eight hours in many manufacturing sectors—was the straightforward product of union pressure and legislative reform. On this view, workers collectively demanded shorter hours, organized strikes and lobbying campaigns, and eventually compelled employers and lawmakers to codify their demands into law. The eight-hour movement, in Rae's account, is essentially a story of political mobilization triumphing over economic resistance.

The sociologist Marion Croft challenges this picture, arguing that Rae's account underestimates the degree to which employers themselves had independent economic reasons to favor shorter hours. Drawing on factory records from textile mills in Britain and steel plants in the United States, Croft contends that managers discovered, often through informal experimentation, that fatigued workers made costly errors, damaged machinery, and produced goods of inferior quality. Shortening the workday, in this view, was not merely a concession to labor—it was also a rational response to the economics of industrial production. Croft further notes that Frederick Winslow Taylor's influential time-and-motion studies, which sought to maximize worker efficiency, provided a managerial language for articulating what factory floors had already been learning by trial and error: that productivity per hour could rise substantially when total hours were curtailed.

Croft acknowledges that her account leaves certain facts unexplained. In industries where fatigue costs were low—clerical work, retail, domestic service—the reduction in hours lagged far behind manufacturing, despite the presence of the same labor unions and legislative pressures that Rae emphasizes. If union pressure alone were the key driver, one would expect a more uniform decline across sectors. The uneven pattern, Croft maintains, is far more consistent with an employer-driven efficiency rationale than with the uniform-pressure model Rae defends.

Yet Croft's own account is not without difficulties. Critics have pointed out that the factory records she draws upon were selectively preserved—mills that engaged in efficiency-minded record-keeping were also more likely to have shortened hours voluntarily, creating a potential bias in her sample. Furthermore, legislative histories reveal that in several jurisdictions the eight-hour workday was mandated for industries—including mining—where productivity-per-hour gains were negligible and fatigue costs were contested. These cases sit awkwardly alongside Croft's efficiency thesis. The most defensible conclusion may be that both Rae's mobilization account and Croft's efficiency account capture real but partial mechanisms: union pressure and employer self-interest reinforced each other in some sectors while operating independently in others, and neither alone suffices to explain the full historical record.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: John Rae's account of the eight-hour movement is the most accurate explanation of the decline in working hours across industrialized nations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Marion Croft's efficiency-based account of the reduction in working hours is superior to Rae's mobilization account because it explains the uneven sectoral pattern of the decline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both union pressure and employer self-interest contributed to the historical decline in working hours, and neither explanation alone fully accounts for the record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Frederick Winslow Taylor's time-and-motion studies were the primary cause of the reduction in the industrial workday during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The decline in working hours was driven mainly by legislative reform, with union activity and employer interests playing only supporting roles.

explanations.correct: The passage introduces Rae's union-pressure account, presents Croft's efficiency-based challenge, and then identifies problems with both, concluding that each captures 'real but partial mechanisms.' The main point integrates all four paragraphs and is captured by C.
explanations.A: Too narrow and incorrect in valence — the passage treats Rae's account as incomplete, not most accurate.
explanations.B: The passage explicitly raises problems with Croft's account in the final paragraph, so calling it 'superior' overstates the author's endorsement.
explanations.D: Taylor's studies are mentioned as a supporting detail within Croft's argument, not as the passage's main claim.
explanations.E: The passage never concludes that legislation was the primary driver; union pressure is one of two partial explanations.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward Croft's efficiency-based account can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement tempered only by a minor empirical quibble

choices.label: B
choices.text: outright rejection on the grounds that her evidence is methodologically flawed

choices.label: C
choices.text: qualified approval, acknowledging that her account captures genuine mechanisms while identifying significant limitations

choices.label: D
choices.text: neutral indifference, treating her account as merely one in a long series of equally valid interpretations

choices.label: E
choices.text: guarded skepticism, suggesting that her account is less plausible than Rae's standard explanation

explanations.correct: The author gives Croft's account substantial, favorable treatment in paragraphs two and three, then raises specific problems in paragraph four, finally concluding that both accounts capture 'real but partial mechanisms.' This is qualified approval with acknowledged limitations.
explanations.A: The final paragraph raises more than a minor quibble — sample bias and the mining-industry counterexample are substantive challenges.
explanations.B: The author does not reject Croft's account; the conclusion explicitly incorporates it as capturing real mechanisms.
explanations.D: The author is not neutral — they take a definite position that both accounts are partially correct.
explanations.E: The author does not treat Croft's account as less plausible than Rae's; both are accorded similar partial validity.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A historical phenomenon is described, a scholarly explanation is introduced and endorsed, and the endorsement is then defended against a series of objections.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A standard scholarly account is presented, a competing account is introduced and supported with evidence, the competing account's own limitations are identified, and a synthesizing conclusion is offered.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing scholarly accounts are introduced simultaneously, their areas of agreement are enumerated, and a third account is proposed as superior to both.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A methodological debate between two historians is described, a resolution is reached by appeal to quantitative data, and the implications of that resolution are explored.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A puzzling historical pattern is identified, a single explanation is developed in detail, and the explanation is shown to account fully for all known evidence.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 presents Rae's standard account. Paragraphs 2–3 introduce and develop Croft's competing account with supporting evidence. Paragraph 4 identifies problems with Croft's account, then offers a synthesis. This matches B exactly.
explanations.A: The passage does not endorse a single account; it concludes that both are partial.
explanations.C: The two accounts are not introduced simultaneously, and no third account is proposed.
explanations.D: No resolution is reached through quantitative data; the conclusion is qualitative and synthetic.
explanations.E: The passage ends by noting that neither account fully explains all the evidence.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Croft draws on which of the following as primary evidence for her argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Legislative records documenting the timing and scope of eight-hour workday laws across multiple jurisdictions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Factory records from textile mills in Britain and steel plants in the United States

choices.label: C
choices.text: Time-and-motion studies conducted by Frederick Winslow Taylor in American manufacturing facilities

choices.label: D
choices.text: Statistical surveys of union membership rates across manufacturing and service-sector industries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wage records from British domestic service and retail industries showing the persistence of long working hours

explanations.correct: Paragraph 2 explicitly states that Croft draws on 'factory records from textile mills in Britain and steel plants in the United States.'
explanations.A: Legislative records are mentioned in the final paragraph as a challenge to Croft, not as evidence she herself deploys.
explanations.C: Taylor's studies are mentioned as a corroborating source that provided managerial language, not as Croft's primary evidence.
explanations.D: No statistical surveys of union membership are mentioned anywhere in the passage.
explanations.E: While lagging hours in domestic service are mentioned, Croft uses the sectoral pattern as an inferential point, not as primary archival evidence she cites.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that the author would agree with which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Union organizing was irrelevant to the decline in working hours in manufacturing industries during the late nineteenth century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mandatory reduction of the workday in the mining industry is difficult to explain on purely efficiency-based grounds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Frederick Winslow Taylor's time-and-motion studies were the decisive cause of the eight-hour movement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The historical record shows that employer self-interest was always the primary driver of shorter working hours, regardless of sector.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The decline in working hours was more rapid in clerical and retail sectors than in manufacturing because fatigue costs were higher in those sectors.

explanations.correct: The final paragraph states that mining is an industry 'where productivity-per-hour gains were negligible and fatigue costs were contested,' and that such cases 'sit awkwardly alongside Croft's efficiency thesis.' This strongly implies the author finds mining-industry legislation hard to explain on efficiency grounds alone.
explanations.A: The passage never dismisses union organizing as irrelevant; Rae's account centers on it and the author treats it as capturing real mechanisms.
explanations.C: Taylor's studies are described as providing a 'managerial language' for existing practices, not as a decisive cause.
explanations.D: The passage explicitly rejects the view that any single driver was always primary, concluding that both mechanisms operated in different combinations.
explanations.E: The passage states the opposite — hours lagged in clerical and retail, where fatigue costs were low, not high.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of the lagging decline in hours in clerical work, retail, and domestic service (third paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: demonstrate that union organizing was entirely ineffective outside of manufacturing industries

choices.label: B
choices.text: provide evidence that supports Rae's uniform-pressure model of labor reform

choices.label: C
choices.text: illustrate the sectoral unevenness that Croft argues is better explained by an employer efficiency rationale than by uniform union pressure

choices.label: D
choices.text: introduce a third explanatory account that neither Rae nor Croft has considered

choices.label: E
choices.text: concede a weakness in Croft's account by identifying industries where her efficiency model also fails to apply

explanations.correct: Paragraph 3 explicitly uses the uneven sectoral pattern — hours lagging in low-fatigue industries despite the same union pressures — to argue that the pattern is 'far more consistent with an employer-driven efficiency rationale than with the uniform-pressure model Rae defends.' The function is to marshal evidence for Croft's position against Rae's.
explanations.A: The passage does not claim unions were 'entirely ineffective' outside manufacturing — only that hours lagged, which is consistent with partial effectiveness.
explanations.B: The sectoral unevenness is presented as a problem for Rae's model, not as support for it.
explanations.D: No third account is introduced in this paragraph.
explanations.E: This paragraph supports Croft's account rather than conceding a weakness in it; the weaknesses appear in the following paragraph.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, would most undermine Croft's efficiency-based account of the reduction in working hours?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Several of the British textile mills whose records Croft examined had been acquired by owners who were also active in labor reform advocacy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Taylor's time-and-motion studies were not widely read by factory managers until well after the eight-hour workday had already been adopted in most manufacturing sectors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Archival research has revealed that manufacturing sectors with the highest rates of worker fatigue injuries were also the sectors where unions were most active and strikes most frequent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In industries where fatigue costs were demonstrably high, the reduction in working hours occurred at the same rate as in industries where fatigue costs were negligible.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Factory owners in the United States were slower to adopt shorter hours than their British counterparts, even when operating in industries with comparable fatigue profiles.

explanations.correct: Croft's core argument is that shorter hours spread faster in industries with high fatigue costs because employers recognized efficiency gains. If hours declined at the same rate regardless of fatigue costs, the efficiency rationale loses its explanatory power — the variation in fatigue costs would predict different rates, but none would be observed.
explanations.A: This complicates Croft's sample but merely introduces a potential confound — it does not directly refute the efficiency mechanism itself.
explanations.B: Taylor's studies are presented as corroborating managerial thinking that was already present, so their late dissemination is consistent with Croft's claim that informal experimentation preceded Taylor's codification.
explanations.C: This actually supports a combined account rather than undermining Croft — it shows high-fatigue industries overlapped with high-union activity, which is compatible with both mechanisms operating together.
explanations.E: National variation in adoption timing would complicate Croft's account but does not directly contradict the fatigue-cost mechanism, which could still operate differently across national regulatory contexts.
